title: Post-Babesiosis Warm Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
population_and_n: Retrospective single-centre cohort (Brigham and Women's Hospital), 86 patients with babesiosis (B. microti) diagnosed January 2009 to June 2016; 18 asplenic; 6 developed warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (WAHA).
abstract_summary: Babesiosis usually causes non-immune haemolytic anaemia that resolves with antimicrobial therapy. After noticing sporadic cases of WAHA after treatment, the authors reviewed all babesiosis patients treated at their centre over 7.5 years for haematological complications within 3 months. Of 86 patients, 18 were asplenic. Six developed WAHA 2 to 4 weeks after diagnosis, by which time all had responded clinically and biochemically to antimicrobials and cleared B. microti parasitaemia. All six were asplenic (P<0.001). All had a positive direct antiglobulin test for IgG and complement C3, warm autoantibodies were identified, and no alternative cause of haemolysis was found. Four of the six needed immunosuppressive treatment. None had prior autoimmunity. The authors conclude that post-babesiosis WAHA occurs in people without prior autoimmune disease and that asplenic patients appear at particular risk. (Paraphrased from the PubMed record as returned by WebFetch.)
key_finding: 6 of 86 babesiosis patients (all 6 asplenic) developed IgG/C3-positive warm AIHA 2-4 weeks after parasitaemia cleared; 4 needed immunosuppression.
corrections: PubMed record (efetch XML) has no CommentsCorrectionsList entries: no erratum, retraction or expression of concern. Publication type: Journal Article only. Note this is the only abstract-level human babesiosis cohort; the 6 WAHA cases are numerically small and the cohort is single-centre and retrospective.

title: Cell-free hemoglobin mediated oxidative stress is associated with acute kidney injury and renal replacement therapy in severe falciparum malaria: an observational study
population_and_n: Prospective observational study of adults (Bangladesh): 107 severe falciparum malaria, 80 uncomplicated malaria, 28 sepsis patients.
abstract_summary: The study asked whether cell-free haemoglobin (CFH) drives oxidative stress and kidney injury in severe falciparum malaria. AKI (creatinine at least 1.5 times expected baseline) was present at enrolment in 62 of 107 severe malaria patients (58%). Patients with AKI had higher admission CFH (geometric mean 8.8 vs 5.1 microM, P=0.018), F2-isoprostanes (56.7 vs 27.8 pg/ml, P<0.001) and isofurans (109.2 vs 41.7 pg/ml, P<0.001). CFH correlated with haemolysis markers, parasite burden (PfHRP2) and F2-isoprostanes. F2-isoprostanes and isofurans were higher in patients who later needed haemodialysis and in fatal cases, and F2-isoprostanes correlated inversely with red cell deformability. Over 72 hours, F2-isoprostanes, isofurans, PfHRP2, CFH and red cell rigidity were independently associated with rising creatinine. Admission F2-isoprostanes, isofurans and deformability were associated with later dialysis. (Paraphrased from the PubMed record as returned by WebFetch.)
key_finding: In 107 adults with severe falciparum malaria, cell-free haemoglobin and lipid-peroxidation products (F2-isoprostanes, isofurans) were higher with AKI and tracked later dialysis need and death.
corrections: PubMed record (efetch XML) has no CommentsCorrectionsList entries. Publication type: Journal Article; Observational Study. Abstract does not name haptoglobin, haemopexin or LDH, so it is the CFH/oxidative-injury comparator, not the scavenger-depletion comparator.

title: Dysregulation of the haem-haemopexin axis is associated with severe malaria in a case-control study of Ugandan children
volume_issue_pages: 14:511 (article number; no page range in record)
population_and_n: Case-control study of Ugandan children with P. falciparum malaria: 87 total (29 uncomplicated, 27 severe malarial anaemia, 31 cerebral malaria); 58 severe cases in outcome analysis (19 fatal, 39 non-fatal); plus mouse experiments (group sizes not in abstract).
abstract_summary: The authors measured the haem-haemopexin axis in 87 Ugandan children with falciparum malaria. Haemin was higher and haemopexin lower in both severe malarial anaemia and cerebral malaria than in uncomplicated malaria (haemin p<0.01; haemopexin p<0.0001). Among the 58 severe cases, higher haemin and cell-free haemoglobin at presentation were associated with death (p<0.05). In mice, cerebral-malaria-susceptible C57BL/6 animals had lower circulating haemopexin than resistant BALB/c animals (p<0.01), and haemopexin-gene-deleted mice had higher mortality than wild-type littermates (p<0.05). The work links depletion of the haem scavenger haemopexin and rising free haem to severe disease and death. (Paraphrased from the PubMed record as returned by WebFetch.)
key_finding: Haemopexin was depleted and free haemin raised in severe malarial anaemia and cerebral malaria; haemin and cell-free Hb predicted death; Hpx-null mice died more.
corrections: Published December 2015, i.e. just before the requested 2016-2026 window; included because it is the best human falciparum study of haemopexin depletion specifically. PubMed record (efetch XML) has no CommentsCorrectionsList entries. Abstract names haptoglobin among plasma measurements but reports no haptoglobin result. Case-control design in children, n modest, and a mouse component.

title: Elevated plasma interleukin-8 as a risk factor for mortality in children presenting with cerebral malaria.
population_and_n: Children with P. falciparum cerebral malaria, southern Benin; n=70 (50 survivors, 20 deaths); CSF multiplex PCR (14 pathogens) used to exclude co-infection; plasma Luminex (17 markers) and urinary assays (7 markers) at inclusion, D3 and D30
abstract_summary: Seventy Beninese children with P. falciparum cerebral malaria were followed to outcome (50 survived, 20 died). Co-infections were excluded by multiplex PCR on cerebrospinal fluid. Seventeen plasma and seven urinary markers of inflammation and oxidative stress were measured on admission and at days 3 and 30. In univariate analysis, TNF, IL-1beta, IL-10, IL-8, CXCL9, granzyme B and angiopoietin-2 were higher, and urinary PGE2 metabolite lower, in children who died. In multivariable logistic models, high admission plasma IL-8 was the main independent risk factor for death (adjusted OR 14.2, P=0.002). Follow-up samples showed markers of resolution (CXCL5, CCL17, CCL22, urinary 15-F2t-isoprostane), and markers tied to neutrophil activation, endothelial activation and damage, and inflammatory/oxidative responses tracked aggravation.
key_finding: In 70 children with cerebral malaria, TNF, IL-1beta, IL-8, IL-10 and CXCL9 were higher in the 20 who died; admission IL-8 was the strongest independent mortality predictor (aOR 14.2).
corrections: None. PubMed CommentsCorrections list is empty (no erratum, retraction or expression of concern); publication type Journal Article.

title: Activated Neutrophils Are Associated with Pediatric Cerebral Malaria Vasculopathy in Malawian Children.
population_and_n: Malawian children with cerebral malaria (Blantyre Malaria Project); abstract gives no n. Per PMC full text: whole-blood transcriptomes from 97 children (64 malarial-retinopathy-positive Ret+CM, 33 retinopathy-negative Ret-CM); plasma neutrophil proteins in 51 Ret+CM vs 25 Ret-CM; autopsy brain samples examined
abstract_summary: The authors compared peripheral whole-blood transcriptomes of Malawian children with cerebral malaria and retinopathy (a marker of cerebral sequestration of infected red cells, Ret+CM) against children with cerebral malaria without retinopathy (Ret-CM). Ret+CM showed upregulation of 103 gene-set pathways, including cytokine, coagulation and extracellular-matrix pathways, and neutrophil transcripts were the most strongly upregulated individual genes. Plasma neutrophil elastase, myeloperoxidase and proteinase 3 (but not lactoferrin or lipocalin) were higher in Ret+CM, while neutrophil chemotaxis was impaired, possibly linked to raised plasma heme. Neutrophils were rare in autopsy brain microvessels and no extracellular traps were seen, implying effects mediated by soluble neutrophil products. Ret-CM children had less inflammation, higher interferon-alpha and Toll-like receptor pathway upregulation.
key_finding: In Malawian children with cerebral malaria, neutrophil transcripts and plasma elastase, MPO and proteinase 3 were higher in those with retinopathy (cerebral sequestration), indicating neutrophil activation linked to severe vasculopathy.
corrections: None. PubMed CommentsCorrections list is empty (no erratum or retraction). Note: abstract omits sample sizes; the n values above come from the PMC full text, not the abstract. Comparison is between two severe-malaria phenotypes, not severe versus uncomplicated; no uncomplicated-malaria or healthy control comparison in the abstract.

title: Whole blood transcriptomics reveals sepsis mortality-associated changes in neutrophil degranulation.
journal: American Journal of Respiratory Cell and Molecular Biology
population_and_n: Critically ill adults with sepsis, prospective observational cohort, University of Pennsylvania; n=161 (60 died within 30 days, 37%); independent validation cohort n=479 with 28-day mortality
abstract_summary: In a prospective cohort of 161 critically ill sepsis patients, whole-blood RNA was collected within 24 hours of ICU admission and profiled by microarray. Gene expression in 30-day non-survivors was compared with survivors, adjusting for age, sex and neutrophil count. There were 1106 differentially expressed genes in non-survivors, including neutrophil granule genes (CEACAM8, ELANE, PRTN3, MPO, CEACAM6, DEFA4, MS4A3) expressed more than 1.8-fold higher despite the neutrophil-count adjustment. The neutrophil degranulation pathway was over-represented in differentially expressed genes in both the discovery and an independent 479-patient cohort, by gene set enrichment, and in four of six co-expression modules correlated with mortality. The authors conclude that neutrophil degranulation genes are involved in sepsis mortality and may be a modifiable target.
key_finding: In 161 ICU sepsis patients, neutrophil granule genes (MPO, ELANE, PRTN3, DEFA4) were over-expressed in 30-day non-survivors independent of neutrophil count, replicated in 479 patients.
corrections: None. PubMed CommentsCorrections list is empty (no erratum or retraction). Publication type Journal Article; Observational Study. Transcript-level (microarray) evidence only; no protein or functional neutrophil assay in the abstract.

title: Severe babesiosis in Long Island: review of 34 cases and their complications.
study_type: human case series (foundational, older; labelled as such because no recent primary human babesiosis study measuring coagulation was found)
population_and_n: 34 consecutive hospitalised adults with severe Babesia infection over 13 years (Long Island, New York, USA), compared with uninfected febrile control patients (control n not given in abstract); 7 had exchange transfusion, 3 died.
abstract_summary: Over 13 years the authors identified 34 consecutive hospitalised patients with severe babesiosis and compared them with uninfected febrile controls. Cases more often had malaise, arthralgia, myalgia and dyspnoea, and more often had thrombocytopenia and abnormal liver function. Forty-one percent developed complications including acute respiratory failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), congestive heart failure and renal failure. Complicated disease was associated with severe anaemia (haemoglobin below 10 g/dL, P=.01) and higher parasitaemia (above 10%, P=.08). Treatment combined clindamycin, quinine, atovaquone or azithromycin; parasitaemia persisted a mean of 8.5 days (range 3-21). Exchange transfusion lowered high parasitaemia in 7 patients. Three patients died. The abstract gives no breakdown of how many patients had DIC and no laboratory coagulation measurements.
key_finding: In 34 severe human babesiosis cases, thrombocytopenia was commoner than in febrile controls and 41% had complications including DIC; complicated disease tracked severe anaemia and high parasitaemia.
corrections: PubMed record checked 2026-10-23: no CommentsCorrections entries, no erratum, no retraction notice.

title: A Novel Assay for Neutrophil Extracellular Trap Formation Independently Predicts Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation and Mortality in Critically Ill Patients.
journal: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
study_type: primary human cohort (prospective, sepsis-predominant ICU population; sepsis comparator, not babesiosis)
population_and_n: 341 consecutive adult ICU patients (UK); strong NET formation found predominantly in sepsis. Sepsis subgroup size not given in abstract.
abstract_summary: The authors built an ex vivo assay in which patient plasma from ICU admission is incubated with isolated neutrophils to semiquantify NET-forming capacity. Among 341 consecutive adult ICU patients, NET formation was absent in 22.0%, mild in 49.9%, moderate in 14.4% and strong in 13.8%, with strong formation mostly in sepsis. After adjustment for APACHE II, the degree of NET formation independently predicted DIC and 28-day mortality, whereas cell-free DNA, myeloperoxidase and myeloperoxidase-DNA complexes did not. IL-8 concentration was strongly associated with NET formation, blocking IL-8 attenuated NETosis, and MAPK activation by IL-8 was identified as a major pathway. The assay measures NET-inducing capacity of plasma rather than circulating NETs.
key_finding: In 341 ICU patients, plasma NET-forming capacity independently predicted DIC and 28-day mortality after APACHE II adjustment; strong NET formation was mainly in sepsis.
corrections: PubMed record checked 2026-10-23: no erratum or retraction. One CommentIn entry (editorial: Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019;200(7):798-799, PMID 31185179), which is commentary, not a correction.

title: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria is associated with circulating ultra-large von Willebrand multimers and ADAMTS13 inhibition.
study_type: primary human cohort (prospective, patients vs controls; foundational, older; labelled as such because more recent human work on ADAMTS13 in malaria is weaker or limited to case reports, meta-analysis and review)
population_and_n: Ghanaian patients with severe P. falciparum malaria (n=20) and cerebral malaria (n=13), plus controls (control n not given in abstract).
abstract_summary: This prospective Ghanaian study of severe (n=20) and cerebral (n=13) falciparum malaria tested whether raised von Willebrand factor (VWF) reflects a functional change. Plasma VWF antigen was raised, and VWF collagen-binding activity was disproportionately raised (medians 7.6 and 7.0 IU/ml in cerebral and severe malaria versus 1.9 IU/ml in controls, p<0.005), correlating with abnormal ultra-large VWF multimers. ADAMTS13 activity was persistently reduced to about 55% of normal (p<0.005). Mixing studies with patient plasma and pooled normal plasma plus recombinant ADAMTS13 showed time-dependent inhibition of ADAMTS13 function. This was not explained by known inhibitors (IL-6, free haemoglobin, factor VIII, thrombospondin-1), so an unidentified inhibitor was suggested.
key_finding: In severe and cerebral falciparum malaria, VWF collagen-binding and ultra-large multimers were raised while ADAMTS13 activity fell to about 55% of normal, with functional inhibition in plasma-mixing studies.
corrections: PubMed record checked 2026-10-23: no CommentsCorrections entries, no erratum, no retraction notice.

title: Intravascular haemolysis in severe Plasmodium knowlesi malaria: association with endothelial activation, microvascular dysfunction, and acute kidney injury.
population_and_n: Hospitalised Malaysian adults with P. knowlesi malaria: 48 severe, 154 non-severe, 50 healthy controls
abstract_summary: The authors studied hospitalised adults with knowlesi malaria and healthy controls. They measured cell-free haemoglobin as a marker of intravascular haemolysis. They also measured the endothelial markers angiopoietin-2 and osteoprotegerin, plus ICAM-1, E-selectin, IL-6, creatinine and lactate. Microvascular reactivity and nitric oxide-dependent endothelial function were assessed as well. Cell-free haemoglobin rose with disease severity and tracked parasitaemia. It was higher than in severe falciparum malaria from the same research group. Cell-free haemoglobin was also linked to angiopoietin-2 and osteoprotegerin. Osteoprotegerin was independently associated with the adhesion molecules, impaired microvascular reactivity and nitric oxide-dependent endothelial dysfunction. Acute kidney injury occurred in 88% of severe cases, and both angiopoietin-2 and osteoprotegerin were independent risk factors for it. The authors propose that haemolysis-driven endothelial activation contributes to end-organ injury. The abstract does not report effect sizes.
key_finding: In severe knowlesi malaria, haemolysis tracked Ang-2 and osteoprotegerin, impaired microvascular and NO-dependent function, and independent risk of AKI (88% of severe cases).
corrections: PubMed XML shows no CommentsCorrections elements (no erratum, retraction or expression of concern).

title: Glycocalyx Breakdown Is Associated With Severe Disease and Fatal Outcome in Plasmodium falciparum Malaria.
population_and_n: Adult inpatients in Indonesia with falciparum malaria: 43 severe, 57 moderately severe, 29 healthy controls (n=129); 3 deaths among severe cases
abstract_summary: This prospective study asked whether breakdown of the endothelial glycocalyx tracks with severity and death in adult falciparum malaria. Urinary glycosaminoglycans were measured by dye-binding assay and by mass spectrometry, and normalised to creatinine. Levels were highest in severe disease (dye assay mean 3.98; mass spectrometry 6.82), intermediate in moderately severe disease (1.78; 4.87) and lowest in controls (0.22; 1.24), with P below 0.001. Within the severe group, the 3 patients who died had higher levels than the 39 survivors (medians 6.72 vs 3.10 by dye assay and 12.15 vs 4.64 by mass spectrometry; P=0.03). Glycocalyx breakdown correlated with parasite biomass and was inversely related to endothelial nitric oxide bioavailability. The authors conclude that glycocalyx degradation is linked to severe disease and fatal outcome.
key_finding: Urinary glycosaminoglycan (glycocalyx breakdown) rose with falciparum severity, was higher in the 3 deaths than 39 survivors, and was inversely linked to endothelial NO bioavailability.
corrections: No erratum, retraction or expression of concern. PubMed lists one CommentIn (editorial: Clin Infect Dis 2019;69(10):1721-1723, PMID 30698670). Mortality comparison rests on only 3 deaths.

title: Angiopoietin-2 outperforms other endothelial biomarkers associated with severe acute kidney injury in patients with severe sepsis and respiratory failure.
population_and_n: 228 adults with severe sepsis and acute respiratory failure (VALID prospective cohort); 141 developed KDIGO stage 2-3 AKI
abstract_summary: This prospective observational study used the VALID cohort of adults with severe sepsis and acute respiratory failure. Of 228 patients, 141 developed severe acute kidney injury (KDIGO stage 2 or 3). Four plasma endothelial markers were measured at enrolment: angiopoietin-2, soluble VE-cadherin, endocan and syndecan-1. All four were higher in patients with severe AKI, but only angiopoietin-2 stayed independently associated with it (odds ratio 6.07 per log increase, 95% CI 2.34-15.78, p<0.001). Angiopoietin-2 also rose with hepatic, coagulation and circulatory organ failure, and was higher in non-pulmonary than pulmonary sepsis. The authors conclude that early endothelial injury, best captured by angiopoietin-2, is linked to sepsis-associated AKI and wider organ dysfunction.
key_finding: In 228 septic patients with respiratory failure, only Ang-2 (not syndecan-1, endocan or sVE-cadherin) independently predicted severe AKI (OR 6.07 per log increase).
corrections: PubMed XML shows no CommentsCorrections elements (no erratum, retraction or expression of concern).

title: Neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL) predicts the occurrence of malaria-induced acute kidney injury.
population_and_n: 39 travellers with imported P. falciparum malaria (Rotterdam Malaria Cohort; 10 with severe malaria); 6 developed AKI (15%)
abstract_summary: Pilot evaluation study of whether structural tubular injury markers (serum NGAL, urine NGAL and urine KIM-1) identify AKI earlier than serum creatinine in imported falciparum malaria. Thirty-nine patients from the Rotterdam Malaria Cohort with stored serum and urine from presentation were included, 10 of whom met criteria for severe malaria. Six (15%) developed AKI. Serum NGAL, urine NGAL and urine KIM-1 all had large areas under the ROC curve for predicting AKI. Urine NGAL performed best: AUROC 1.00 (95% CI 1.00-1.00), PPV 1.00 (95% CI 0.54-1.00) and NPV 1.00 (95% CI 0.89-1.00). The authors conclude NGAL and KIM-1 have good diagnostic performance for malaria-associated AKI and that larger studies are needed to show superiority over creatinine.
key_finding: At presentation, urine NGAL (AUROC 1.00) and urine KIM-1 predicted subsequent AKI in 39 imported falciparum patients (6 AKI cases); sample is small and the cohort non-endemic.
corrections: PubMed record checked (efetch XML, 2026): no CommentsCorrections entries, so no erratum or retraction is listed. Publication types: Evaluation Study; Journal Article. Caution: n=39 with only 6 AKI events, so the perfect AUROC is likely optimistic; chosen because it is the human study that measures the same urinary NGAL and KIM-1 as the canine papers.

title: Comparative Outcomes of Babesiosis in Immunocompromised and Nonimmunocompromised Hosts: A Multicenter Cohort Study.
population_and_n: 225 adults with laboratory-confirmed babesiosis (2009-2023), multicentre US; 112 immunocompromised and/or asplenic/hyposplenic (ICAH) vs 113 immune-intact
abstract_summary: Multicentre retrospective cohort of 225 adults (mean age 66 years, 36% female) with laboratory-confirmed babesiosis, comparing 112 patients with immunocompromise or asplenia/hyposplenia (ICAH) against immune-intact patients. ICAH patients had higher median peak parasitaemia (2.8% vs 0.9%, P<0.0001) and more complications, including AKI (24% vs 11%, P=0.016) and ARDS (11% vs 4%, P=0.041). They more often needed red cell transfusion (31% vs 17%) and exchange transfusion (18% vs 6%), had longer treatment (median 27 vs 10 days), and higher 12-month all-cause mortality (7% vs 1%) and recurrence (8% vs 0%). Haematological malignancy and B-cell-depleting therapy predicted recurrence. AKI is reported as a complication only; no kidney biomarkers or mechanism were examined.
key_finding: In 225 human babesiosis patients, AKI occurred in 24% of immunocompromised/asplenic vs 11% of immune-intact patients, alongside higher peak parasitaemia and more ARDS.
corrections: PubMed record checked (efetch XML, 2026): no CommentsCorrections entries, so no erratum or retraction is listed. No PMCID in record. Selected as the best-powered primary human babesiosis study with an explicit AKI outcome; it is not a mechanistic renal study, and the AKI definition is not stated in the abstract.

title: Pulmonary Manifestations of Babesiosis and Predictors of Mortality from a Quaternary Care Center in Westchester, New York.
population_and_n: 147 hospitalised adults with confirmed babesiosis (63 severe, 41 ICU, 10 deaths), Westchester Medical Center, New York, 2006-2023; single-centre retrospective
abstract_summary: This single-centre retrospective study reviewed 147 hospitalised adults with confirmed babesiosis (2006-2023) to describe pulmonary involvement, using logistic regression for factors tied to severe disease and death. Of the 147, 63 were severe, 41 needed ICU care and 10 died. Respiratory symptoms (cough, dyspnoea, oxygen need, respiratory failure) occurred in 42%, and 55 patients had abnormal chest radiographs (infiltrates, effusions). Parasitaemia of 10% or more was present in 75% of severe cases. Severe disease was associated with age 70 or older, severe dyspnoea, radiographic abnormality, WBC above 5000, haemoglobin 8 g/dL or lower and raised creatinine. Mortality was associated with age 70 or older, encephalopathy, acute kidney injury, severe dyspnoea at admission, abnormal chest radiograph and intubation. Exchange transfusion did not correlate with outcome. Lyme seropositivity was 28%. The authors conclude that pulmonary symptoms and abnormal radiographs are common and signal worse outcomes.
key_finding: In 147 hospitalised babesiosis adults, 42% had respiratory symptoms; abnormal chest radiograph, severe dyspnoea and intubation were associated with mortality, as was concurrent acute kidney injury.
corrections: No CommentsCorrections entries (errata, retraction or correction notices) in the PubMed XML record for PMID 40333147, checked 2026-10-23.

title: Babesiosis as a cause of acute respiratory distress syndrome: a series of eight cases.
population_and_n: 22 adult B. microti patients admitted to a medical ICU (Lower Hudson Valley, New York, 2008-2016); 8 developed ARDS; retrospective
abstract_summary: The authors reviewed adults admitted to a tertiary-hospital medical ICU in New York between 2008 and 2016 to describe ARDS complicating Babesia microti infection. Of 22 babesiosis ICU patients, 8 (36.4%) had ARDS. Six of the 8 (75%) developed ARDS after anti-babesial therapy had started, although those patients also had longer symptom duration before treatment than the two who developed ARDS earlier (7.5 vs 4.5 days, p=0.34). Three of the 8 (37.5%) died without ARDS resolution, versus 14.3% mortality among the 14 patients without ARDS (p=0.31). Survivors tended to be younger (54.6 vs 74.0 years, p=0.07), and 3 of 5 survivors avoided mechanical ventilation. Non-survivors had markedly higher SOFA scores (12.3 vs 6.0, p=0.0006). The authors raise, but cannot resolve, whether parasite killing contributes to ARDS onset.
key_finding: 8 of 22 ICU babesiosis patients developed ARDS, mostly after antiparasitic therapy began (confounded by longer symptom duration); 3 of 8 died.
corrections: No CommentsCorrections entries (errata, retraction or correction notices) in the PubMed XML record for PMID 30585748, checked 2026-10-23. No PMC full text. Small retrospective series; the mortality difference (37.5% vs 14.3%) was not significant.

title: Release of endothelial activation markers in lungs of patients with malaria-associated acute respiratory distress syndrome.
study_type: primary human cohort (post-mortem case-control immunohistochemistry); comparator pathogen, not babesiosis
population_and_n: Post-mortem lung sections from Thai P. falciparum patients with alveolar oedema (MA-ARDS), P. falciparum patients without alveolar oedema, and uninfected accidental-death controls; group sizes not reported in abstract
abstract_summary: Malaria-associated ARDS (MA-ARDS) is poorly understood. Because endothelial activation drives other malarial complications, the authors stained post-mortem lung sections for von Willebrand factor (VWF) and angiopoietin-2 (ANG-2) in three groups: P. falciparum patients without alveolar oedema, P. falciparum patients with alveolar oedema (MA-ARDS), and uninfected controls with normal lungs, using semi-quantitative scoring. Oedematous alveoli and intravascular VWF and ANG-2 staining were significantly higher in MA-ARDS than in both control groups. VWF in alveolar septa and the lining of large vessels was lower in MA-ARDS, which the authors interpret as Weibel-Palade body release. ANG-2 was raised in the septa of infected patients without oedema, and ANG-2-positive leukocytes were increased in alveoli in both infected groups. The data indicate marked pulmonary endothelial activation in MA-ARDS.
key_finding: Post-mortem lungs from falciparum patients with alveolar oedema showed raised VWF and ANG-2 in oedematous alveoli, indicating pulmonary endothelial activation and Weibel-Palade body release.
corrections: No CommentsCorrections entries (errata, retraction or correction notices) in the PubMed XML record for PMID 31796023, checked 2026-10-23. Group sizes not stated in the abstract; semi-quantitative IHC on post-mortem tissue, so cause-effect cannot be inferred.

title: Alteration of Blood Lactate Levels in Severe Falciparum Malaria: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
population_and_n: 30 studies of patients with severe falciparum malaria (pooled n = 30,202 cases); 9 studies compared severe with uncomplicated malaria (1568 vs 1693 cases); 6 studies compared deaths (272) with survivors (1370).
abstract_summary: The review asked whether blood lactate, the usual driver of metabolic acidosis in severe malaria, is higher in severe than uncomplicated disease and higher in patients who die. PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus were searched (793 records retrieved, 30 included), with quality appraised by the Jadad scale and STROBE, and random-effects pooling with meta-regression and subgroup analysis. Pooled mean lactate in severe malaria was 5.04 mM (95% CI 4.44-5.64; I2 99.9%). Lactate was higher in severe than uncomplicated malaria (mean difference 2.46 mM; 95% CI 0.85-4.07; nine studies) and higher in fatal than surviving severe malaria (mean difference 2.74 mM; 95% CI 1.74-3.75; I2 95.8%; six studies). The authors conclude lactate differs markedly by severity and outcome, and call for studies of its prognostic value for identifying patients at high risk of developing severe malaria or dying.
key_finding: Blood lactate was about 2.7 mM higher in patients who died of severe falciparum malaria than in survivors (six studies), with very high heterogeneity.
corrections: PubMed record checked 2026-10-23 (efetch XML): no CommentsCorrections entries (no erratum, retraction or expression of concern). Publication type Journal Article/Review; the abstract describes a systematic review and meta-analysis. Chosen as a review (not a primary study) because it pools 30 studies and is the only paper that directly pools the survivor versus non-survivor lactate contrast; heterogeneity (I2 about 96-100%) limits precision of the pooled estimates. Primary alternatives reviewed: PMID 38243243 (n=1674 children, cerebral malaria, admission lactate >5 mmol/L OR 2.49 for death) and PMID 34172046 (n=5425 children, AQUAMAT secondary analysis, hypoglycaemia OR 5.16 for severe metabolic acidosis).

title: Cortisol and adrenal androgens as independent predictors of mortality in septic patients.
population_and_n: 139 consecutive adults with severe sepsis or septic shock, Spain (prospective cohort; hormones measured within 24 h of onset).
abstract_summary: This prospective single-country cohort tested whether basal cortisol, DHEA, DHEAS and their ratios predict mortality in septic patients. Hormones were sampled in the first 24 h; ROC analysis and adjusted logistic regression assessed in-hospital, 28-day and 90-day death, with comparison against lactate, CRP, SOFA and APACHE II. Cortisol was the best predictor, with AUCs of 0.758 (in-hospital), 0.759 (28-day) and 0.705 (90-day), whereas for 28-day mortality SOFA, APACHE II, lactate and CRP gave AUCs of 0.644, 0.618, 0.643 and 0.647. Cortisol above 17.5 ug/dL carried adjusted odds ratios of about 10.1 (in-hospital) and 9.5 (28-day) for death. Adrenal androgen associations were weak; the cortisol/DHEAS ratio was the best 90-day predictor (AUC 0.737). Cortisol was concluded to be the strongest early prognostic marker.
key_finding: Admission cortisol above 17.5 ug/dL predicted in-hospital and 28-day death (adjusted OR about 10) and outperformed SOFA, APACHE II and lactate in 139 septic patients.
corrections: PubMed record checked 2026-10-23: no CommentsCorrections entries (no erratum or retraction). Sepsis (non-parasitic) cohort, so a comparator for hypercortisolaemia as a mortality marker, not an equivalent of babesiosis; single cohort of moderate size, no external validation. Larger or newer sepsis cortisol studies exist (e.g. PMID 42617202, 2026, multicentre retrospective) but were not read in full.

title: Thyroid hormone levels as a predictor marker predict the prognosis of patients with sepsis.
population_and_n: 929 adult septic patients identified from the MIMIC-III intensive care database (703 favourable and 226 unfavourable outcome); retrospective database analysis.
abstract_summary: Using the MIMIC-III critical-care database, the authors identified 929 septic patients to test whether admission thyroid hormone levels relate to short-term outcome. Variables with P below 0.1 on univariate analysis entered a multivariable binary logistic regression, and discrimination was assessed by AUROC. Thyroxine (T4) was significantly lower in patients with an unfavourable outcome (P < 0.01), and lower admission T4 was associated with poor outcome (OR 0.556, 95% CI 0.41-0.75). A combined model of free T4, T4 and SAPS II reached an AUROC of 0.82 for ICU survival, above free T4 alone (0.65), T4 alone (0.71) and SAPS II (0.70-0.72), so thyroid hormones added predictive information to the clinical score. The authors conclude low serum T4 is a predictive marker of short-term sepsis outcome.
key_finding: Lower admission thyroxine was independently associated with poor short-term outcome in 929 septic patients, and added to SAPS II in a combined model (AUROC 0.82).
corrections: PubMed record checked 2026-10-23: no CommentsCorrections entries (no erratum or retraction); no PMCID in the record. Retrospective database study with limited detail on thyroid-testing selection (hormones measured only in a subset of patients is likely but not stated in the abstract). The abstract does not report TSH; for the TSH-unchanged point, a separate sepsis study (PMID 41827956, n=149, 2026) and a meta-analysis (PMID 30237537, 2018) were read but not selected.

title: Parasite histones are toxic to brain endothelium and link blood barrier breakdown and thrombosis in cerebral malaria.
population_and_n: Malawian children with cerebral malaria (P. falciparum): circulating histones in patient serum, brain MRI, postmortem brain sections, plus in vitro human brain endothelial assays. Exact n is not stated in the abstract and was not verified from full text.
abstract_summary: The authors ask how P. falciparum causes the endothelial disruption seen in paediatric cerebral malaria, where microvascular thrombosis and blood-brain barrier (BBB) breakdown are linked to fatal brain swelling. Circulating extracellular histones, of host and parasite origin in roughly equal measure, were significantly raised in cerebral malaria patients, and higher levels went with brain swelling on MRI. In postmortem brain sections, histones co-localised with infected erythrocytes sequestered in small vessels, which suggests local release at schizont rupture. Luminal histone staining coincided with thrombosis and vascular leakage. Patient sera and purified parasite histones disrupted barrier function and killed cultured human brain endothelial cells. Anti-histone antibody and non-anticoagulant heparin blocked this effect. The authors propose histones as a link between sequestration, thrombosis, BBB breakdown and brain swelling.
key_finding: Histone levels tracked MRI brain swelling, and postmortem histone staining colocalised with sequestered parasitised cells, thrombosis and vascular leakage in human cerebral malaria brain.
corrections: No CommentsCorrections elements (erratum, retraction or correction links) in the PubMed XML record, checked 2026-10-23. Bibliographic data verified from the PubMed record.

title: Increased brain microvascular hemoglobin concentrations in children with cerebral malaria.
population_and_n: 46 Malawian children with cerebral malaria (Blantyre coma score of 2 or less, retinopathy-positive); comparators 33 with uncomplicated malaria and 29 healthy children
abstract_summary: Brain swelling is linked to death in cerebral malaria, but it is unclear whether it reflects cerebral oedema or vascular congestion, which affect tissue haemoglobin differently. Using near-infrared spectroscopy, the authors measured cerebral microvascular haemoglobin concentration in 46 Malawian children with cerebral malaria, 33 with uncomplicated malaria and 29 healthy children. Concentrations were higher in cerebral malaria than in uncomplicated malaria (median 145.2 vs 82.9 uM, P = 0.008) and correlated with the MRI brain swelling score (r = 0.37, P = 0.03). Detrended fluctuation analysis showed lower self-similarity of the haemoglobin signal in cerebral malaria (0.63 vs 0.91, P < 0.0001), which suggests impaired cerebral blood flow regulation. The authors conclude that excess blood volume, possibly from vascular congestion, may contribute to brain swelling.
key_finding: Cerebral microvascular haemoglobin was higher in paediatric cerebral malaria and correlated modestly with MRI brain swelling (r=0.37), which suggests vascular congestion contributes to swelling.
corrections: No CommentsCorrections elements (erratum, retraction or correction links) in the PubMed XML record, checked 2026-10-23. Bibliographic data verified from the PubMed record.

title: Neurologic Complications of Babesiosis, United States, 2011-2021.
population_and_n: 163 adults hospitalised with laboratory-confirmed babesiosis at Yale-New Haven Hospital, Connecticut, USA, January 2011 to October 2021 (retrospective record review)
abstract_summary: Babesiosis is caused by intraerythrocytic protozoa and its full neurologic spectrum, underlying neuropathophysiology and risk factors are poorly understood. The authors reviewed the medical records of adults admitted to Yale-New Haven Hospital with laboratory-confirmed babesiosis between January 2011 and October 2021. Among 163 patients, more than half had at least one neurologic symptom during admission. The most frequent symptoms were headache, confusion or delirium, and impaired consciousness. Neurologic symptoms were associated with high-grade parasitaemia, renal failure and a history of diabetes mellitus. The authors advise clinicians in endemic areas to recognise neurologic presentations of babesiosis. The study describes frequency and associations only and does not measure any mechanism such as sequestration, imaging change or barrier disruption.
key_finding: Over half of 163 hospitalised babesiosis patients had neurologic symptoms, associated with high-grade parasitaemia, renal failure and diabetes; no mechanism was assessed.
corrections: No CommentsCorrections elements (erratum, retraction or correction links) in the PubMed XML record, checked 2026-10-23. Bibliographic data verified from the PubMed record. Species is not given in the abstract (US babesiosis is overwhelmingly B. microti, which is an inference, not a stated fact). Not a mechanistic study.

title: Cardiac Complications of Human Babesiosis.
study_type: primary human cohort (retrospective single-centre record review)
population_and_n: 163 adult inpatients with smear- and/or PCR-confirmed babesiosis, Yale-New Haven Hospital, Jan 2011 to Oct 2021
abstract_summary: The authors reviewed records of all adults admitted with confirmed babesiosis to one US hospital over about ten years. Of 163 patients, 32 (19.6%) had at least one cardiac complication in hospital. The commonest were atrial fibrillation (9.4%), heart failure (8.6%), QTc prolongation (8.0%) and cardiac ischaemia (6.8%). Neither cardiovascular risk factors nor pre-existing cardiac disease were significantly associated with developing a cardiac complication. Patients with a cardiac complication more often had high-grade parasitaemia (>10%), and had longer hospital and ICU stays and higher mortality than those without. The authors conclude that cardiac complications are common in acute babesiosis and that the link between babesiosis severity and cardiac outcomes needs further study. The abstract does not report troponin values or echocardiographic data.
key_finding: About one in five hospitalised babesiosis patients had a cardiac complication, associated with parasitaemia >10%, ICU stay and higher mortality.
corrections: No erratum, retraction or expression of concern in the PubMed record (no CommentsCorrections entries). Limitations to carry forward: troponin and echo results are not in the abstract, and complications are clinically coded (AF, HF, QTc, ischaemia) in older adults, so they do not equate to myocardial injury measured by biomarker.

title: Assessment of Myocardial Function and Injury by Echocardiography and Cardiac Biomarkers in African Children With Severe Plasmodium falciparum Malaria.
population_and_n: 104 children aged 3 months to 12 years with severe falciparum malaria (61 with severe malarial anaemia), Mbale Regional Referral Hospital, Uganda
abstract_summary: This prospective study followed 104 Ugandan children with severe falciparum malaria, nested in the FEAST fluid-bolus trial context, with echocardiography at presentation and 24 hours. Cardiac troponin I and BNP were measured at presentation. Troponin I exceeded 0.1 ng/mL in 50 children (48%), while median BNP was normal. Cardiac index was higher in severe malarial anaemia than in other severe malaria (6.89 vs 5.28 L/min/m2) and normalised by 24 hours after transfusion and antimalarial treatment; it correlated inversely with haemoglobin. Only 4 children (3.8%) had depressed systolic function (EF <45%). Six died, and none developed pulmonary oedema or biventricular failure. The authors conclude that elevated cardiac index is a physiological response to anaemia, that systolic function is preserved in over 96%, and that troponin elevation does not correlate with cardiac dysfunction.
key_finding: Troponin I was raised in 48% of children with severe malaria, yet systolic function was preserved in over 96% and troponin did not track dysfunction.
corrections: No erratum, retraction or expression of concern in the PubMed record. The only CommentsCorrections entry is a published commentary (CommentIn, Pediatr Crit Care Med 2018;19(3):262-263, PMID 29499020). The abstract contains an apparent unit typo (haemoglobin '< 5 mg/dL', presumably g/dL) and 'n equals to 50' phrasing; these are transcription oddities, not corrections.

title: Early high-sensitivity troponin elevation and short-term mortality in sepsis: a systematic review with meta-analysis.
population_and_n: 17 studies, 6242 adults meeting Sepsis-3 criteria, with short-term mortality 16.9% to 53.8%
abstract_summary: The review searched PubMed, Scopus and Embase for studies relating early high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) to short-term mortality in adults with Sepsis-3 sepsis. Seventeen studies with 6242 patients were pooled with random-effects models. Non-survivors had higher hs-cTn than survivors (standardised mean difference 0.87, 95% CI 0.41-1.33). Elevated versus normal hs-cTn was associated with higher mortality (unadjusted OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.41-2.25). In studies that adjusted for confounders, the association disappeared (aOR 1.06, 95% CI 0.99-1.14). The authors conclude that troponin is raised in sepsis non-survivors and is linked to mortality, but is not an independent predictor of death, consistent with a marker of overall illness severity.
key_finding: Raised hs-troponin in sepsis tracks mortality crudely (OR 1.78) but not after adjustment (aOR 1.06), so it behaves as a severity marker, not an independent predictor.
corrections: No erratum, retraction or expression of concern in the PubMed record. The only CommentsCorrections entry is a published commentary (CommentIn, Crit Care 2025;29(1):118, PMID 40102885). Chosen over the 2023 meta-analysis (PMID 37773717, unadjusted HRs, older troponin assays, no Sepsis-3 restriction) because it separates crude from adjusted effects.

title: Risk Factors for Severe Infection, Hospitalization, and Prolonged Antimicrobial Therapy in Patients with Babesiosis.
journal: The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene
population_and_n: 128 patients with smear- or real-time PCR-confirmed Babesia microti infection, collected over 16 years.
abstract_summary: This study evaluated 128 patients with smear- or real-time PCR-confirmed B. microti infection over 16 years, aiming to define prognostic indicators of serious complications needing hospitalisation or prolonged therapy. Patients with asplenia or immunocompromising conditions were more likely to have severe infection, need hospitalisation, or receive prolonged antimicrobial courses (all P<0.01). Nausea or vomiting, diarrhoea and hyperbilirubinaemia (all P<0.01) were predictive of severe infection, hospitalisation and prolonged therapy. Patients with concurrent Lyme disease were less likely to need hospitalisation, and had similar severity and antibiotic duration compared with those without Lyme disease. The abstract reports P values rather than effect sizes.
key_finding: In 128 B. microti patients, asplenia or immunocompromise, GI symptoms and hyperbilirubinaemia predicted severe infection, hospitalisation and prolonged therapy; concurrent Lyme reduced hospitalisation.
corrections: PubMed CommentsCorrections list is empty (no erratum or retraction, checked 2026-10-23). Chosen as the older, smaller supplement to the two 2025 papers because it is the only candidate that links asplenia/immunocompromise and hyperbilirubinaemia (a haemolysis/liver marker) to severity in one primary cohort. It is a 2017 study with n=128, and the abstract reports only P values (no effect sizes) and no parasitaemia analysis.
